extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of mathematics; general mathematical problem-solvers
extracted.subtask_description: A guide to mental operations, questions, and procedures useful when solving mathematical problems (both 'problems to find' and 'problems to prove'), emphasizing variation, analogy, auxiliary constructions, induction, and heuristic vs rigorous reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The remaining questions in the list have a common aim, the VARIATION OF THE PROBLEM. There are different means to attain this aim as GENERALIZATION, SPECIALIZATION, ANALOGY, and others which are various ways of DECOMPOSING AND RECOMBINING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary the problem to gain new perspectives or auxiliary elements: generalize to access new procedures, specialize to simpler cases, use analogy to related contexts, decompose and recombine parts. Variation can lead to auxiliary elements or more accessible auxiliary problems; it is essential to problem-solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have you seen it before?
rubrics_metrics.description: Have you seen the same problem before, or the same problem in a slightly different form? Any feature of the present problem that played a role in a previous solution may play a role again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search memory for previously solved problems or theorems that are related. Even a negative answer can trigger useful recollections. If a related solved problem is found, examine how its solution or method might be used (directly or after adaptation) in the present problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a formerly solved related problem (use its result or method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Here we succeeded in recollecting an old problem B of which we know the solution but we do not know yet how to use it. We ask: Could you use it? Could you use its result? Could you use its method?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try to link the new problem A with a known problem B by introducing corresponding auxiliary elements; then attempt to use B's result or method. Example: solving the circumscribed sphere-of-tetrahedron problem by analogy with the circle circumscribed about a triangle, introducing perpendicular-bisecting planes analogous to perpendicular bisectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invent (or look for) an auxiliary problem
rubrics_metrics.description: When you cannot use a formerly solved problem, invent a related auxiliary problem B that you suspect you can use even if you do not yet know how to solve B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devise auxiliary problems that, if solved, would yield the desired result for the original problem. Distinguish cases where you know B's solution (then you must find how to apply it) versus when you invent B (you know how to use it but must solve it). Introducing the right auxiliary problem can transform an intractable problem into a tractable one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce auxiliary elements (construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Should you introduce some auxiliary element in order to make [use of a known result] possible?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce geometric or algebraic auxiliary elements (e.g., lines, triangles, planes, loci) suggested by analogous simpler problems. Even if some parts of the introduced element are not yet known, foreseeing how they can be obtained constitutes essential progress and gives a plan of attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic reasoning (provisional discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic reasoning is reasoning not regarded as final and strict but as provisional and plausible only, whose purpose is to discover the solution of the present problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heuristic arguments freely to explore, guess, and discover ideas; display them openly and tastefully. Do not mix heuristic reasoning with rigorous proof, and do not pass heuristic arguments off as proofs. Heuristics often prepare rigorous arguments and contain useful germs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish induction (empirical) from mathematical induction (proof technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction (discovering general laws by observation of particular instances) is different from mathematical induction (a method used in mathematics to prove statements about integers); there is very little logical connection although they are often used together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical induction to conjecture general laws (observe patterns, test cases). Use mathematical induction to convert a conjecture into a rigorous proof by proving a base case and the passage n → n+1. Ensure the assertion is explicit enough to test the passage from n to n+1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test conjectures by checking cases and passage to next integer
rubrics_metrics.description: We may test the first case not tested yet, and more effectively check whether the formula remains true when we pass from any value n to n+1; subtract and simplify to verify the transition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify conjectures by computing additional specific cases, and where applicable, check the transition from n to n+1. Such tests can provide strong support and, in the constructive pattern of mathematical induction, can enable a full proof. Use computations, simple manipulations, and difference arguments as checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's paradox (try stronger/general statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more ambitious plan may have more chances of success. The stronger theorem is easier to master than the weaker one; the more comprehensive theorem may be easier to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't shy away from more general or stronger formulations; passing from a less precise to a more precise statement can make proofs accessible. However, the generalization must be grounded in a real vision, not mere pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foresee features of the result (anticipate what to expect)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is good to foresee any feature of the result for which we work. An important feature is the number of solutions the problem admits (uniqueness etc.). Ask: Is it possible to satisfy the condition? Is it sufficient, redundant, or contradictory?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make provisional guesses about features like uniqueness, existence, redundancy, or contradiction. Such anticipations guide which directions to pursue and help prioritize simpler, informative questions early on; abandon these questions when their answers seem too difficult to obtain and not worth the effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look at the unknown (respice finem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Look at the end. Remember your aim. Think of what you are desiring to obtain. Look at the unknown. The last two versions are adapted to problems to find and to problems to prove respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus attention on the unknown (the nature/category of what is sought: length, angle, volume, point, etc.). By considering the unknown first, restrict possible auxiliary constructions and identify the simplest familiar problems having the same unknown to adapt methods or results from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize the conclusion for 'problems to prove'
rubrics_metrics.description: For problems to prove we look at the conclusion, consider our theorem emphasizing the conclusion, and try to think of a familiar theorem having the same or a similar conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving a theorem, concentrate on the desired conclusion and search for known theorems with the same conclusion (or similar). Plan to reduce the problem to proving those known results or to introduce auxiliary elements that allow application of them (e.g., introduce triangles to prove equality of angles via congruence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the simplest familiar problems with the same unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: In simple cases, the most elementary problems with the same unknown are usually sufficient. Looking at the unknown restricts choice to the most elementary and familiar relevant problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by trying to adapt very simple classical problems that share the same type of unknown (e.g., triangle side/angle problems for length/angle unknowns). This economy of choice helps to find an efficient starting plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma as provisional assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma means 'auxiliary theorem.' We assume B provisionally, postponing its proof, and go ahead with the proof of A. Such a theorem B is assumed and is an auxiliary theorem to the originally proposed theorem A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lemmas by assuming an auxiliary result temporarily to see how it would help the main proof; later return to prove the lemma. This approach helps structure complex proofs and guides which auxiliary facts are worth proving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear notation and geometrical figures
rubrics_metrics.description: In all sorts of problems, but especially in mathematical problems which are not too simple, suitable NOTATION and geometrical FIGURES are a great and often indispensable help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt convenient, unambiguous notation and draw clear diagrams; these often reveal relations, simplify arguments, and make auxiliary constructions and computations manageable.

rubrics_metrics.name: When you cannot solve the problem, seek consolation with easier related problems
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot solve the proposed problem do not let this failure afflict you too much but try to find consolation with some easier success, try to solve first some related problem; then you may find courage to attack your original problem again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stuck, deliberately attempt simpler or related problems to gain momentum, insights, and confidence. Such intermediate successes can reveal methods or auxiliary ideas applicable to the original problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek similar unknowns if same-unknown problems are unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: If we have no formerly solved problem having the same unknown, try to find one having a similar unknown; problems of the latter kind are less closely related but may be valuable guides nevertheless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt methods from problems with similar but not identical unknowns (e.g., use known results about curved surfaces similar to the sphere to approximate or inspire methods). Treat these as guides and be prepared to adapt or extend them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study heuristic broadly (logical, psychological, and experiential basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern heuristic endeavors to understand the process of solving problems, especially the mental operations typically useful in this process. A serious study should take into account both the logical and the psychological background and unbiased experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not neglect historical insights, psychological aspects (determination, hope, subconscious work), or observational experience of others solving problems. Heuristic study aims at general, subject-matter-independent features that can improve teaching and practice.
